notespost: What I find particularly interesting about this track is the way it seems to disregard many of the established conventions of mixing and mastering. To me, this is perhaps the first time we are given a clear sense of what Tim Henson and his collaborators are ultimately seeking to achieve with this new stylistic direction. I find the approach genuinely intriguing. Many may consider it unusual, but I believe music would become remarkably dull if artists were no longer willing to explore unfamiliar territory and experiment with new ideas.

Natori is widely known for his more rhythmic, energetic, hard-hitting, and exuberant sound. On his album ‘Theater’, however, there is a slower and more emotional song that he wrote for his sibling’s wedding, which people still jokingly reference to this day precisely because it feels so unlike him. This track, however, shows that he is more than capable of writing this kind of music in his own distinctive way. What I find remarkable is that he has managed to evoke something I had previously only experienced in the music of Fujii Kaze: a feeling that somehow makes you smile while carrying an almost unbearably painful, heart-wrenching undertone at the same time. To me, this track stands remarkably far apart from what we have come to expect from Natori, yet his musical identity remains unmistakably present throughout. It has become one of my personal favourites of his.

My very first thought when I discovered this artist was simply, please… tell me he was the producer, haha. The atmosphere this song creates is so extraordinarily complex, almost beyond human, that I immediately felt it must have required a truly generational musical mind behind it. After looking into it a little further, my intuition proved correct: it was indeed Kenshi’s work.

Hikaru Utada initially felt somewhat unexpected to me within the context of the entire concept, but after several listens, it becomes remarkably clear that there could hardly have been a more fitting collaboration for this piece. In time, you begin to appreciate not only the subtlety of her contribution, but also the remarkable humility and sensitivity with which she serves the music itself.
